surface: tare — standalone microsite for Tare. It covers /apps/tare/ (Persuade) plus /apps/tare/privacy/ and /apps/tare/support/ (Read variants of the same world). No /alternatives/ page targets Tare: it has no alternatives_to, and grep finds no page with slug tare. The alternatives Read variant is therefore specified for future pages only.

dossier.mechanism: Tare is a wordless lever-law puzzle. You hang weights numbered 1–9 on the notched hooks of a hanging mobile until every beam balances at once. A beam balances when weight × distance from the pivot is equal on both sides, and a nested beam pulls with its whole load at its hook. Any beam carrying a hidden “?” weight sways instead of tilting, so hidden values can only be deduced from picture-card clues, never read off the scale. There are 80 handmade levels, each machine-proven to have exactly one answer.
dossier.audienceScene: Two groups, on iPhone or iPad. The first is logic-puzzle players: who_for names sudoku, nonograms and Kakuro. The second is families who want a game with nothing to read. They play offline on a train, a plane or underground, or on the sofa in the evening with the sound on. Before launch the page is unlisted (sitemap:false, status upcoming). It is reached only from the App Store listing (App Store Connect uses /apps/tare/ as the marketing and support URL) and from the in-app Privacy link. After launch, visitors arrive from Google and AI answers for ‘balance puzzle game’, ‘offline puzzle game no wifi’ and ‘puzzle game no ads’, mostly on a phone.
dossier.culturalHome: Four strands. (1) Pencil puzzles and their publications: Nikoli's hand-made, one-solution puzzles, and puzzle books with a Rules box, an Example and the answers at the back. (2) The lever everyone met first: the seesaw, the school pegged number balance, Cuisenaire rods. (3) Wordless instruction and notation: assembly booklets, play-by-colour songbooks, Isotype. (4) The game's own painted-toy world, Signboard Sky. The founder note records that the developer turned away from a ‘quiet museum piece — hairline beams on warm paper’ because it was ‘tasteful and dull’.
dossier.mustProve: In one viewport, with no screenshot to lean on, the page must show a playable mobile that balances by weight × distance, a hidden “?” weight whose beam won't reveal it, and a picture card that lets you deduce it. It must also show that the game is wordless, runs on iPhone and iPad, has 20 levels free and the other 60 for $2.99 once, has no ads and collects no data. The official App Store badge must be in reach.
dossier.categoryDefault: The puzzle-game landing page: full-bleed key art or a pastel ‘zen puzzle’ gradient behind a tilted iPhone; a rounded casual-game face (Fredoka, Baloo); ‘Download now’; a row of icon feature tiles (80 levels · offline · no ads · hints); a screenshot carousel; a star strip; two pricing cards; an FAQ accordion. The incumbent adds a cream ground, Newsreader, a purple accent and the split hero. For Tare it also currently points at an icon and a QR code that do not exist.
dossier.predictableOpposite: The gallery Calder: a white or warm-paper page with one hairline mobile drawn in thin black line, serif captions and acres of space. This is exactly the ‘Quiet Gallery’ build the developer made first and then discarded. The founder bio says so, and the front-matter comment calls those captures superseded.
dossier.literalReading: Read literally, ‘Tare’ is the scale's zeroing button or the empty weight stencilled on a container, and ‘hanging mobile’ is a Calder in a museum. One candidate spends the name's literal reading: #7, the brass weight set and the pan balance. The Calder reading is left out entirely because it is the developer's own discarded direction. The roll did not deal #7.
evidence: _apps/tare.md facts. Status and visibility: status ‘upcoming’ with sitemap:false, so the page is unlisted (every listing filters on status ‘live’). Platforms: iPhone and iPad only, iOS 26.5+, portrait, no Mac. Category: games. app_store_url is https://apps.apple.com/app/id6806255929, and the Smart App Banner app-id=6806255929 is already emitted. Pricing: price.model free; price.value ‘20 levels free · $2.99 unlocks 60 more’; schema_price 0, schema_high_price 2.99, 2 offers. Plans: Chapter I ‘Free’ (highlight) and Chapters II–IV ‘$2.99 once’, plus a plans_footnote. Release fields: first release 2026-09-14, last updated 2026-09-14, version 1.0. There are no ratings, so no stars and no aggregateRating.

Blocks Tare HAS: hero (pre_headline; headline ‘Hang the weights. Balance every beam. Deduce the rest.’; secondary; a long subheadline; cta_label ‘Play Chapter I free’; cta_subline; alt), quick_answer, who_for ×5, who_not_for ×4, value_points ×4, features ×8, how_it_works (intro + 4 steps), faq ×13, privacy (tracking false, account false, data_collection none, 7 notes, policy_url), founder (Organization ‘Lagerland Apps’, bio, 5 signals, response time), support email, plans ×2, show_body + about_heading. Blocks it does NOT have: spotlight, screenshots, comparison_table, roadmap, training_vocabulary, insight gallery, plateau_disclosure, coach_cta, related_journal, alternatives_to.

No image assets exist. assets/icons/tare.png, assets/screenshots/tare/, assets/qr/tare.svg and assets/og/tare.png are all missing, and the board's assets/tare/ folder is empty. This follows the owner's decision of 2026-09-14: ‘no images yet’. The current build already references qr/tare.svg and the missing icon. Every style therefore runs on type, colour, structure and code-drawn demonstration.

The app's own look is known from words only. The founder bio says ‘every screen was redrawn as a painted toy on a sky-blue board’. Front matter describes chalk-white beams with notches 1–4 a side; weights 1–9 showing a numeral plus domino pips; “?” soap bubbles; picture cards pinned above the board and a shelf below; gold stars, sparks and the sun on a solve; a chord in which heavier is lower; and four canvases (Morning Sky, Twilight Meadow, Deep Sea, Evening Stars). The art direction is named ‘Signboard Sky’. The older ‘Quiet Gallery’ captures are superseded and must not be used.

The developer's own reasoning, from the founder bio: the museum-piece version was ‘tasteful and dull’. The rule he defends above all is that a beam with a secret sways instead of tilting: ‘Without that, the hidden weights are a guessing game.’ The founder signals: no networking code; all 80 levels machine-proven; every picture drawn in SwiftUI code, with sounds the only recorded assets; VoiceOver, Dynamic Type, High contrast and Reduce Motion from the first release.

No alternatives page targets Tare. No journal post mentions it: the two grep hits are ‘stare’ and ‘stares’. It has no entry in _data/app_enrichment.yml, _data/transparency.yml or _data/testimonials.yml.

Privacy page front matter has a seo block, overview, data_collection none, data_storage (SwiftData and UserDefaults on the device only; Lantern use and session counts are never written), third_parties (the Apple purchase, Family Sharing, the rating prompt and four outbound links), sensitive_data (no permissions; the motion sensor is read live for parallax), children, changes, contact_email and back_url, with sitemap:false. The support page has a seo block, a slug and the support email, also with sitemap:false.
Two URLs are hard-coded elsewhere: the app links /apps/tare/privacy/, and App Store Connect uses /apps/tare/ as the marketing and support URL. Both permalinks are fixed from day one.

Sibling boards were read before ranking. Soon uses dawn-sky bands and a sun. LiftLog A colour-codes weights by value, and LiftLog C uses the Munich ’72 pictograms. Millrace uses an amber millrace, ThinkFun challenge cards and a golf scorecard. Rightsplit A uses deli-scale labels. No sibling uses a puzzle book or a glockenspiel, or the faces Recursive, Zen Maru/Kaku Gothic, Tilt Warp or Andika.

candidates.name: The pencil-puzzle book (Nikoli lineage): Rules box, worked Example, numbered puzzles, answers upside down
candidates.why: who_for names sudoku, nonograms and Kakuro players, and Nikoli's creed (hand-made puzzles, one solution, solvable by logic rather than guessing) is Tare's value point almost word for word. How it carries the mechanism: the Rules box states the weight × notch rule and the “?” rule. A worked Example shows 2 at notch 2 balancing 4 at notch 1. Puzzle No. 1 is solved in pencil on the page itself, and its answer is printed upside down at the foot, which doubles as the no-JS proof.

candidates.name: The wordless assembly booklet: flat-pack furniture and brick-toy instructions
candidates.why: Everyone has built something from a booklet with no words, and Tare teaches its rule the same way. How it carries the mechanism: the parts-inventory box becomes the shelf of numbered weights (‘1× 3, 1× 2, 1× ?’). A sub-assembly callout frame with an arrow becomes a nested beam whose whole load acts at one hook. The booklet's ✓/✗ comparison panels become the picture cards and the full-but-wrong shudder. The page would use no brand marks and no mascot figure.

candidates.name: Cuisenaire rods and Gattegno's Silent Way, with the school pegged number balance
candidates.family: classroom manipulative (coloured number rods, plastic maths balance)
candidates.why: Generations met numbers as coloured lengths (white 1 to blue 9), and Gattegno taught with the rods in silence. The pegged school balance is weight × peg in plastic. How it carries the mechanism: each weight is drawn as its rod, so pull reads as length × notch. The picture cards become rod trains (red + red = purple, which is ? = 2 + 2). The silent method stands for the wordless onboarding.

candidates.name: Signboard Sky: the game's own painted board at page scale
candidates.family: the app's own interface (painted toy on a sky-blue board)
candidates.why: This is the developer's own redrawn world, the one App Store visitors meet first, and the founder note explains why it replaced the quiet paper look. How it carries the mechanism: chalk-white notched beams, painted weights with numeral and pips, “?” soap bubbles, pinned picture cards and the shelf are already the mechanism's own objects. The page becomes one level the visitor solves, with the rest of the page hanging below it as a cascade.

candidates.name: Isotype picture statistics (Neurath and Arntz)
candidates.why: Neurath's ‘Words divide, pictures unite’ is Tare's nothing-to-read promise as a 1930s doctrine, and its descendants, airport and Olympic pictograms, are known to everyone. How it carries the mechanism: a weight of 6 becomes six counted units, so balance shows as counted rows × distance, and the picture cards are already Isotype equations. It is weaker on the physical sway, and LiftLog's Munich ’72 programme sits right next door.

candidates.name: The play-by-colour glockenspiel and its songbook
candidates.family: musical instrument and notation (toy glockenspiel, colour-dot songbook, Orff classroom bars)
candidates.why: The songbook lets children play without reading music, as Tare lets anyone play without reading words, and Tare really gives every weight a note (heavier is lower) and makes a solved mobile ring out in one chord. How it carries the mechanism: nine bars stand for weights 1–9, with 9 the longest and lowest. A level is written as a chord of coloured numbered dots, the “?” is the one bar that won't sound, and balance is something you hear. It is weaker on deduction and risks a nursery register.

candidates.name: The brass weight set in its fitted box and the two-pan balance (the literal ‘tare’)
candidates.family: measuring instrument (fitted weight box, pan balance, the scale's TARE)
candidates.why: The name is a weighing word, and a fitted box of graduated brass weights is the shelf of pieces made precious. How it carries the mechanism: weights sit in their stepped holes (the shelf), and the beam balance shows equality. But a pan balance has equal arms, so it cannot show distance from the pivot, which is the core of Tare. Rightsplit's deli-scale labels also already hold the ‘tare’ scale. This is the name's literal reading, spent once here.

styles.label: The Painted Board
styles.lineage: Tare's own ‘Signboard Sky’ art direction, as the front matter and the founder note describe it. Every screen is redrawn as a painted toy on a flat sky-blue board: chalk-white beams with notches 1–4 a side; weights 1–9 painted with a numeral and domino pips; “?” soap bubbles; picture cards pinned above the board; a shelf of pieces below; gold stars and the sun on a solve. The style reads all of this through the single-stroke casual sign painting the direction is named after. No Signboard Sky capture exists in the repo yet, so the page builds the board from those words.
styles.thesis: The page is one Tare level at page scale. The headline is the ceiling rail, and a real mobile hangs from it that the visitor can solve before reading a word of copy. Every section below hangs from the same chalk string, forming one balanced cascade. It refuses the game page's key art, tilted phone and row of icon tiles. It also refuses the developer's own discarded museum look of hairline beams on paper.
styles.scene: A puzzle player on a phone in daylight, on a train or by a window, looking at the same flat cerulean board the game opens on (Morning Sky) → light. One drenched daylight scheme; color-scheme: light.

palette.role: Board: the Signboard Sky cerulean. It is the page ground edge to edge. Chalk text on it reaches 5.0:1, so no lighter blue may ever carry text.
Chalk: the headline, body text on the board, beams, strings and picture-card stock.
Shelf: the hero shelf plank, the sticky shelf bar and the footer. Chalk on it is 10.8:1 and yellow is 7.0:1.
Weight paint: the painted weights, the grade stars, the sun disc and the outer focus ring. As a graphic it is 3.3:1 against the board.
Ink: numerals and pips on weights (9.5:1), text on white cards (14.5:1) and the inner focus ring.
Bubble film: the film of the “?” bubble at 35% under a chalk rim, and the reduced-motion sway trace. It is 3.2:1 against the board.

World canvases, used only in the chapter ledger: Twilight Meadow #3C6E57 (chalk 5.9:1), Deep Sea #0E4A5C (9.8:1) and Evening Stars #241C4F (15.5:1). Morning Sky is the board itself. All three must be re-matched to the app at launch.

type.display: Recursive, variable: @fontsource-variable/recursive, latin ‘casl’ file (CASL 0–1 × wght 300–1000, 109 KB). It is the page's only font file. Set at CASL 1, wght 850: the H1 is 84px/0.98 on desktop and 34px/1.02 on mobile, centred, in chalk. Section heads are 44/30px. Weight numerals use wght 900 on the painted weights.
type.text: The same file at CASL 0.25, wght 420. Body is 19px/1.6 (17px on mobile) at a 62ch measure, chalk on the board or ink on white cards. It also sets FAQ answers and picture-card copy.
type.utility: Recursive at CASL 0, wght 700, with tnum, for real arithmetic and figures: 3 × 2 = 6 = (4 + 2) × 1, the notch numbers 1–4, and $2.99.
type.rationale: The art direction is named Signboard, and Recursive's Casual axis was drawn from single-stroke casual sign painting. The same brush that paints the weights' numerals can therefore set the headline, and turning the axis down gives a calm reading text from one file. No static Fontsource cut carries the CASL axis, so production and mocks must both serve the variable file.

Liquid renders it only when assets/qr/tare.svg exists in site.static_files. That file is absent until launch, so before launch the shelf holds the badge alone.

visitorPath: The board (hero): the wordmark and the pinned-card nav; the H1 as the ceiling rail; the playable demo mobile with its ‘? = 2 2’ card and the demo label; the shelf with the pieces, the badge, price.value and cta_subline. The QR card joins at launch.

Quick Answer: the first thing hanging below the shelf. It is a large white picture card pinned where the string meets it, ink on white at 64ch, marked speakable. Its foot carries the trust line: iPhone & iPad · iOS 26.5+ · no ads · no account · no network code · no data collected.

#how-it-works, One rule: the how_it_works intro in chalk at 28px, then one big chalk beam showing ‘a 2 at the second notch balances a 4 at the first’ (2×2 = 4×1, in tnum). The four steps hang from four hooks of one long beam, numbered 1–4 because the sequence is real (HowTo schema).

#secret, The scale can't be cheated: value point 1 beside two looping beams. One is an honest beam tilting under a 3 and a 2; the other is a “?” beam swaying. Below them, the three picture-card kinds are pinned as the game uses them (equals, heavier, balanced on unequal arms), each drawn in miniature with its one-line meaning from the features text.

Three promises on one beam: value points 2–4 (one answer, no timer, nothing to read). Each hangs at a notch distance inverse to its text length, so the beam visibly balances. This is the page's lever-law layout rule.

The click and the Lantern: the click feature beside a static solved mobile. Then the Lantern's three hint steps in their real order: card, then one hidden value, then a ghost. Then the star grades Hung · Unshaken · Once as three labelled gold stars. Nothing is gated, and no rating stars appear anywhere.

#chapters, Four chapters, one purchase: four hanging canvases on one long beam. They are The Hang · Morning Sky · free; The Secret · Twilight Meadow; The Cascade · Deep Sea; and The Exhibition · Evening Stars. Each has 20 levels and its one-line description from the body. Under them, the two plans hang on either side of the string: Chapter I Free (highlighted) and Chapters II–IV $2.99 once, each with its feature list. Then come the plans_footnote (chapter-order rule, Family Sharing, restore) and the badge.

Built for every player, and quiet by design: one weight drawn large with its numeral and pips. Beside it, the accessibility feature (VoiceOver tree, Dynamic Type, High contrast at 4.5:1, Reduce Motion and Reduce Transparency) and the sound, haptics and appearance switches.

Who it's for and who it isn't: the five who_for lines hang on the short arm of one beam, near the string; the four who_not_for lines hang on the long arm. The longer list hangs closer, so the beam balances.
#about: the about_heading H2 and the show_body markdown on a long white card at 64ch. It covers the rule, ‘The rule that makes it a logic puzzle’, the four chapters, and ‘What it does not do’.

The maker's note: the founder bio set large in chalk (‘Tare started as a quiet museum piece…’) under the Lagerland mark. The five signals follow as a plain list, then the response-time line and a mailto link.
#faq: the 13 questions, each opening with a small “?” bubble. Opening the <details> pops the bubble into a filled chalk dot, and the answer hangs below it.

#privacy, Nothing collected: data collection none, tracking false, account false, and the seven privacy notes. Links go to the privacy policy, to support, and to /transparency/ (Tare is not on the record yet; see notes).
Quick reference: the ai-canonical <details> on a white card, open by default and present in the DOM.

The bottom weight: the last and heaviest piece of the cascade is a short shelf with the badge, price.value and cta_label. Below it come other Lagerland apps (computed from site.apps where status is live), the maker and freshness line (Built by Lagerland Apps · version 1.0 · first released · last updated, from release.*), and the shared ‘A Lagerland app’ strip.
styles.navigation:
Desktop: four pinned picture cards at the board's top right, white stock with a yellow pin and ink text. They link to How it plays (#how-it-works), Chapters & price (#chapters), Questions (#faq) and Privacy (#privacy). The card for the current section hangs straight while the others keep their tilt. The ‘Tare’ wordmark returns to the top.
Mobile: one ‘Contents’ card opens a <details> sheet in the shelf colour, with the same four links plus Download.
Further down the page, the chalk string doubles as a progress cue: the current beam's pivot becomes a filled yellow pin. There is no separate rail.
Focus: a 3px #FFC94A outline outside a 2px #0B2A4A ring, visible on the board, the shelf and white cards. DOM order is reading order.
styles.signatureInteraction:
Hang it yourself: the hero's playable level, drawn in inline SVG.
Input: weights and hooks are real <button>s. Pieces can be dragged (Pointer Events, with a 60px snap like the app), tapped, or moved by keyboard: Enter picks a piece, the arrow keys move between hooks, and Enter hangs it.
Physics: beams rotate about their pivot by clamp(net torque × 2.5°, ±9°). Any beam carrying the unsolved “?” sways ±3° on a 3.2s loop instead. While a piece is held, the picture card that mentions it lifts 4px. A full but wrong board shudders once (±4px, 360ms), with no red.
The solution: 3 on the left at notch 2; on the right at notch 1, the sub-beam with ? at notch 1 and 2 at notch 2. The sums are 3×2 = 6 = (4+2)×1, and 4×1 = 2×2.
The solve: the sway stops and the beams settle with one overshoot. The bubble pops to show 4. Three labelled star grades appear (Hung, Unshaken, Once), scored honestly from the visitor's moves. A flat sun disc rises in the board's top-right corner. An aria-live line narrates each move.
No JS: the SVG prints in its solved state, the arithmetic is the caption and the shelf is empty. The pieces UI exists only under html.js.
Reduced motion: there is no sway. An unsolved “?” beam stays level, with a dashed chalk outline and the text ‘won't settle until you know the ?’. A wrong board shows the line ‘Full, but not balanced’ instead of shuddering, and reveals are instant.
styles.motionGrammar: Pendular only. Anything that moves either rotates about a pivot or drops on a string; nothing slides sideways or fades in from nowhere. Beams settle over 420ms on cubic-bezier(.3,1.35,.5,1), with one overshoot. Under html.js, each section drops 16px and settles from 1° to 0° once (480ms) as it enters. The sticky shelf rises 64px over 260ms. There is no parallax and no scroll-scrubbing. prefers-reduced-motion turns all of it off. All content is in the HTML and visible before any script runs.

styles.assetsNeeded: No raster assets. Beams, weights, bubbles, cards, stars and the sun are all inline SVG/CSS, and the demo level is authored above. Production needs the @fontsource-variable/recursive ‘casl’ latin file (109 KB), because the static Fontsource cuts used by the mock board have no Casual axis. At launch: re-match the board, weight-paint and bubble colours to the Signboard Sky tokens or captures, and add the QR (scripts/generate-qr.py) and the icon.
styles.risk:
Familiarity: this is the closest of the three to the category canon (a game page in the game's own art). Only the working level and the cascade topology keep it from being key art, so a build that turns the demo into a static picture fails.
Colour accuracy: the board is authored from words, so its colours may not match the app until Signboard Sky captures exist. The superseded Quiet Gallery shots must not leak in.
Sibling overlap: Soon's First Light also has a sky and a sun. Here the sky is one flat board with no bands and no horizon, and the sun appears only on a solve.
Accessibility: a drag-and-drop SVG must be fully operable by keyboard and VoiceOver, with named beams, hooks and pieces that mirror the app's VoiceOver tree. Chalk on #2172B8 is 5.0:1, so no lighter blue may carry text.
Stars: on a page with no ratings, the gold stars must stay labelled grades (Hung · Unshaken · Once) and never appear near the badge.
Font budget: the 109 KB font file is most of the budget.
styles.memoryTest: The puzzle page where the headline was the ceiling and a mobile hung off it. I hung the 3 and the 2, the card said the bubble was two 2s, everything stopped swaying and the sun came out, and the download badge sat on the shelf with the pieces.

fixes.text: Re-derive every visitorPath from the world's own reading order, and enforce two rules. (1) Within a surface, no two styles may share the relative order of more than two of {price, screenshots, comparison, privacy record, founder, FAQ}. (2) At least one style per surface must change GROUPING, not just order: for example, FAQ split into the sections it answers, who_for/who_not_for folded into the price, or the privacy record as the opener. styles.label: Answers Upside Down
styles.lineage: Nikoli's pencil-puzzle publishing: Puzzle Communication Nikoli (Tokyo, since 1980; the publisher that named Sudoku) and its pencil-puzzle books. Every puzzle is hand-made by a credited setter and must have one solution reachable by logic. Each puzzle type opens with a framed Rules box and a solved Example, and the answers are at the back. styles.thesis: The page is Tare's own puzzle-book page: a Rules box, then Puzzle No. 1 to solve in pencil before any feature list, with the answer printed upside down at the foot. It treats the visitor as a solver, the way Tare treats its player. It refuses the game hero (key art, phone, feature tiles). It also refuses the broadsheet puzzle page (hairlines, italic serif, mono labels) by printing in rounded gothic and one lime ink.

styles.signatureInteraction:
Solve it in pencil. Puzzle No. 1 is printed, so its beams never move.
Entering a number: tap or focus an empty hook circle, then a piece in the pencil strip. The number writes itself into the circle in Klee One graphite with a 240ms left-to-right clip wipe.
Working: pencilled working appears beside each beam, ‘3 × 2 = 6’ on one side and ‘(? + 2) × 1’ on the other. Once the clue card has been read, the working adds ‘? = 2 + 2 = 4’.
Checking: when every circle is filled and the puzzle balances, a pencil tick appears with ‘Turn to the answers’ (a link to #answers). If it doesn't balance, the working shows the uneven sides in graphite (‘6 ≠ 5’), with no red and no buzzer, and an eraser clears the entries.
The “?” rule: print cannot sway, so the rule is taught in the Rules box and in a small ‘sways’ diagram.
No JS: the puzzle prints empty, as in a book. The full answer and working sit upside down at the foot of the page; they are in the DOM, and screen readers read them upright. A CSS-only checkbox (‘Turn the page’) rotates the answer upright.
Reduced motion: numbers and working appear instantly, with no wipe.
styles.motionGrammar: Print doesn't move; only the pencil does. Entries and working write in from left to right with 200–300ms clip wipes. The current thumb tab extends 8px over 160ms, and the running foot rises over 200ms. There are no section reveals, no parallax and no hover theatre. Everything is visible on load, and reduced motion removes the wipes.

Familiarity: this is the most familiar of the three. ‘Puzzle game → puzzle book’ can be guessed from the category, and many runs would land here.
Drift: it slides into the broadsheet puzzle page (rut c) the moment hairlines, an italic serif or mono labels appear. The rounded gothic and the lime discipline are the style.
No physics: in print, beams never tilt or sway. Tare's most important rule is therefore told and diagrammed rather than felt, and the page undersells the painted, physical feel the developer rebuilt the game for.
Lineage, not costume: no Nikoli name, logo or puzzle-type names appear on the page.

styles.label: Nine Bars, One Chord
styles.lineage: The diatonic toy glockenspiel and its play-by-colour songbook. Its rainbow enamel bars are riveted onto two felt rails that converge as the bars shorten, so the longest bar is the lowest note, and each bar is stamped with its number. Songs are written as rows of coloured numbered dots so children who can't read music can play. Also in the lineage: Orff Schulwerk classroom barred instruments and Boomwhackers' tuned-by-length colour tubes. All of it is read through Tare's own rule: every weight has its own note, heavier is lower, and a solved mobile rings out in a single chord.
styles.thesis: The page writes Tare in play-by-colour notation. There are nine bars, one per weight, with 9 the longest and lowest. The demo mobile is drawn as coloured note-dots that ring their chord only when every beam balances, and the “?” is the one note that won't sound. Balance becomes something you hear. It refuses the game landing's key art and feature tiles, and the floating pastels of zen-puzzle pages.
styles.scene: A player at home after dark with the sound on, earbuds in and the room lights low: the hour Tare's Evening Stars canvas is made for → dark. Claret case felt as the ground, with enamel bars and warm-white type; color-scheme: dark.

palette.role: Case felt (claret): the page ground. Warm white on it is 15.4:1.
Warm white: headlines, body text, beams, strings and the focus ring.
Felt dust: secondary text, captions, notch ticks and the dashed outline of the muted dot (9.3:1).
Rail felt: the two felt rails, the sticky keyboard bar and the footer. Warm white on it is 16.6:1.
Bar ink: the numerals and pips stamped on every bar and note-dot. It reaches at least 4.0:1 on all nine bar colours.

The bar ramp, from lowest to highest note: 9 #E8452C, 8 #F28A1E, 7 #F6C21C, 6 #6DBE45, 5 #1FA58F, 4 #2C8FD6, 3 #5468E0, 2 #9A63D6, 1 #E86FA8. Each is at least 3.5:1 against the felt. These colours appear only where a weight value appears.
Muted bar: the “?” token, felt-covered, with a warm-white “?” at 9.6:1. A 2px dashed #D9B9C4 outline makes it read against the felt.

type.display: Tilt Warp 400 (@fontsource/tilt-warp, static, 12 KB; the variable file's 3D-rotation axes are not used). The H1 is 64px/1.04 on desktop and 34px/1.05 on mobile. Section titles are 40/28px. It also sets every numeral stamped on a bar (30px) or in a 44px note-dot (22px).
type.text: Andika 400/700 (@fontsource/andika, 18–19 KB each). Body is 19px/1.6 at 62ch in warm white. Nav and price lines use 700; captions are 15–16px in felt dust.
type.utility: No separate utility face. The arithmetic (2 × 2 = 4 × 1) is set in Tilt Warp numerals at 22px.
type.rationale: Play-by-colour notation depends on round, heavy, monoline lining figures that sit centred in a dot or stamped on a bar. Tilt Warp's soft, sturdy forms give that stamp without a nursery wobble. SIL drew Andika for people learning to read, with an unambiguous a, I, l and 1. The songbook exists so non-readers can play, and Andika keeps the words just as easy. About 49 KB in all.

materials: Claret case felt #34121F as the page ground, in flat colour.
Nine enamel bars with rounded 8px ends and two felt-dust rivets each, resting on two converging #24101A felt rails and stepping down in length from 9 to 1.

The muted “?” token: felt-covered #5A3443 with a dashed felt-dust outline.
Warm-white 3px beams with notch ticks and 1.5px strings, drawn as notation rather than as toys.
The song card: a clue card outlined in 2px warm white that quotes the pieces as mini dots.

styles.signatureInteraction:
Ring it level. The demo is a real level written in note-dots.
Input: tap (or press Enter on) a token, then a hook; dragging works too.
Physics: beams tilt honestly by torque (±6°), and any beam carrying the unsolved “?” sways instead.
Sound while playing: with sound on, every placed note sounds its pitch. The “?” is silent, so the instrument won't give it away either.
The level: 6 on the top beam's left notch 1. On its right notch 1 hangs a sub-beam with 2 at notch 2 and ? at notch 1. The sums are 2×2 = 4×1 and 6×1 = (2+4)×1. The card reads ? = 2 + 2.
The solve: the beams settle, and the ? dot takes bar 4's blue and flies onto bar 4. Bars 6, 2 and 4 light and strum from low to high, then sound together: a C-major chord (G3, C4, E4) on the page's illustrative pentatonic mapping, from 9 = C3 up to 1 = G4. The tones are synthesized in Web Audio, with no audio files. A full but wrong board gives one felt thump and a shudder, with no red. Any bar can be tapped to hear it, except the muted one.
No JS: the mobile prints in its solved state, with the chord written as three note-dots and the arithmetic in words. The instrument is a static drawing with numerals and pips.
Reduced motion: no sway, shudder or strum; bars light in place. Sound still works when switched on, because sound is not motion.
Sound is off by default and never autoplays.
styles.motionGrammar: Struck, not swung. A sounding bar vibrates ±1.5px for three decaying cycles (240ms), and its light fades over 900ms like a ringing note. Beams tilt fast with a short decay rather than a long swing. Sections enter with no motion at all; the page stays still until it is played. The sticky keyboard rises over 240ms. Reduced motion removes the vibration and the decay animation but keeps the state changes.

styles.risk:
Register: it can read as a preschool toy page. A rainbow xylophone can make a ‘math logic puzzle for adults’ look like a toddler app. Tilt Warp, the claret felt and restraint (colour only where a weight value appears) have to carry the adult register, and the mock has to prove they do.
Invented detail: the note-per-weight rule is real, but the page's pitches and its nine colours are invented. The game's weights show a numeral and pips, and its colours are unknown. Both are labelled, and every dot keeps its numeral and pips.
Sound: it must stay opt-in, so many visitors will meet the signature silently and only see the bars light.
Dark ground: the felt must not slide into near-black-plus-neon. Claret is a colour, the bars are matte and nothing glows.

fixes.text: Re-derive every visitorPath from the world's own reading order, and enforce two rules. (1) Within a surface, no two styles may share the relative order of more than two of {price, screenshots, comparison, privacy record, founder, FAQ}. (2) At least one style per surface must change GROUPING, not just order: for example, FAQ split into the sections it answers, who_for/who_not_for folded into the price, or the privacy record as the opener. World-native examples: tare-b sets Puzzle No. 1 before the Rules and puts price and answers at the back like a book. studio-a, allpaid-c and rightsplit-a open with the record (bin label, statement, label data) before any feature. soon-b prints the fare and stub (price) on the face, first. gymlogger-x-c shows the plateau formula before any offer. xiangqiful-c files each FAQ as a margin question on the entry it concerns. observa-b ends on 'past issues' (release notes) instead of a closing CTA block. The maker/freshness line and the shared footer strip may stay common.

rightsplit-c keeps oxblood, the app's own maroon. Re-felt tare-c in a colour no surface uses, e.g. deep olive (~#33361F); Tare's Evening Stars indigo works only if soon-a is not chosen. Remove the hanging mobile from tare-c's hero. The nine bars on their converging rails become the one playable object across the width, and the level is written as a play-by-colour song line on the song card, solved in notation.

Add one production task to every style: a one-off script in scripts/ (already excluded from the build, so it is not a deploy build step) that commits derivatives. Icons at 64, 128 and 256px (WebP plus a PNG fallback, about 15 KB or less at 128). Screenshots at 400w, 800w and 1200w WebP (about 40, 90 and 160 KB or less). The studio mark as the clean SVG that studio a/b/c already ask for. Front matter keeps the original paths; one include maps them to the derivatives and emits width/height, srcset/sizes, loading=lazy and decoding=async (eager plus fetchpriority=high only for a single hero image).

Make it a global contract: html { scroll-padding-top: var(--sticky-top); scroll-padding-bottom: var(--sticky-bottom) }, so focus and anchors never land under a bar. Allow one sticky element per edge, pad the bottom bar with env(safe-area-inset-bottom), and on viewports shorter than 600px hide the top strip while the bottom bar is showing.

Gate every App Store element on status: wrap the badge, the sticky bar, the QR, cta_label/cta_subline and the apple-itunes-app meta in {% if page.status == 'live' %}. Before launch, render one plain status line in the world's own type, with no Apple artwork and no 'download' verb, e.g. 'Tare is not on the App Store yet. This page holds its rules, privacy and support.' State the price as 'At launch: 20 levels free · $2.99 unlocks 60 more'. Mock the pre-launch state for the owner, and show the live state only as a toggle.
Print 'first released' only when status is live. Before launch, print 'Version 1.0 in preparation · page updated {{ release.last_updated }}'.

Before build, add a tare row (manifest_source: pending; tracking_domains 0; third_party_sdks 0; network_calls none; data_leaves_device no, all from the front-matter privacy block) and deep-link /transparency/#tare. Until that row exists, the privacy block must say 'Not yet on the transparency record; added at launch' rather than imply a verified entry.
